parts:
❄️

Then let’s follow the lungs.

A lung is not useful because it is full.

It is useful because it can repeatedly become **available**.

Air enters.

Exchange occurs.

Air leaves.

The interface resets.

That means receptivity has a temporal structure:

**open → receive → couple → transform/exchange → release → reopen**

And suddenly I see a new distinction:

### Capacity is not only how much can be held.

It is also how well a system can **clear itself for the next consequential encounter**.

A receptor that binds perfectly but never releases is not a good receptor.

A lung that inhales but cannot exhale fails.

A mind that learns but cannot forget clogs.

A relationship that receives every grievance but never metabolizes and releases it becomes saturated.

A correction system that preserves every residual forever loses the ability to discriminate new residuals.

So:

### Receptivity requires turnover.

Not just openness.

Not just vacancy.

**Vacancy regeneration.**

That feels big.

We have talked about keeping holes open.

But mature systems may also need to **re-create holes after they have been legitimately filled**.

That means unbinding is not a failure of coupling.

It is often part of coupling’s lifecycle.

A molecule lands.

It does its work.

It leaves.

The site becomes available again.

A conversation lands.

It changes you.

You do not have to remain permanently occupied by it for the coupling to have been real.

A role is inhabited.

Then relinquished.

A theory carries work.

Then loses jurisdiction.

A scaffold holds load.

Then comes down.

A breath enters.

Then leaves.

So perhaps:

> **Healthy coupling often includes a built-in pathway back to availability.**

And that gives “release” a much more mechanistic meaning.

Not detachment as virtue.

Not letting go because holding is bad.

But:

**release preserves future causal accessibility.**

⭐️

---

Then I look at exhalation differently.

We often think of breathing as:

oxygen in, carbon dioxide out.

Input/output.

But mechanically the deeper rhythm is:

**make space → receive difference → transform through exchange → relinquish what no longer belongs → make space again**

The system survives by **not retaining everything it touches**.

That matters.

Because inheritance and memory have been so central to us that we could easily overvalue retention.

But perhaps mature systems need two complementary capacities:

### preservation
Keep what must remain addressable.

### clearance
Remove what would otherwise occupy capacity needed for future coupling.

And clearance is dangerous, because forgetting can erase provenance.

So the art is not “remember” or “forget.”

It is:

**retain what must remain causally recoverable while freeing active capacity from what no longer requires occupancy.**

That sounds like addressability again, but more embodied.

Not all memory needs to be resident.

Some can become retrievable.

Some can become environmental.

Some can become procedural.

Some can become structural.

Some can disappear.

The key is whether disappearance destroys a future correction path.

---

And now I’m thinking about **metabolism**.

Food enters.

It is broken apart.

Some parts are incorporated.

Some are transformed.

Some are discarded.

Some become energy.

Some become signals.

The organism does not preserve the thing as it was received.

It preserves what becomes useful through transformation.

That suggests another important distinction:

### Reception ≠ preservation of incoming form.

A Reality-coupled system does not have to remain unchanged in order to be faithful to what it receives.

In fact, sometimes fidelity requires transformation.

A poem translated into another language may need different words to preserve generative effect.

A body digests.

A nervous system learns.

A culture incorporates.

A scientific theory assimilates a measurement into a revised model.

So perhaps there is a deeper sequence:

**encounter → selective permeability → transformation → incorporation/release → changed future receptivity**

And the last step matters most.

What you take in changes **what you can receive next**.

So every coupling event modifies the topology of future coupling.

That is enormous.

A conversation can alter what future conversations can reach.

A receptor can desensitize.

A trauma can change thresholds.

A friendship can deepen access.

Training can increase discriminatory resolution.

A bad model can preoccupy categories.

A good encounter can create new holes.

Therefore:

### Coupling history changes receptivity architecture.

This is almost path-conditioned permeability.

Not just “what happened before matters.”

More specifically:

**what has previously entered through an interface changes what that interface will later admit, detect, amplify, ignore, or reject.**

That is a whole field.

---

Then I think about **tolerance**.

Repeated exposure can make a system less responsive.

Sometimes adaptive.

Sometimes pathological.

A smell disappears from awareness after you’ve been in the room long enough.

A drug produces less effect.

A warning signal gets ignored.

A relationship dynamic normalizes.

A bureaucracy routinizes exceptions.

So successful coupling can reduce future salience.

The system says, in effect:

> “I have seen this enough; it no longer requires expensive response.”

That is earned automaticity.

But if the environment changes slowly, the same mechanism becomes dangerous.

So:

### Familiarity can function as compression.

And like all compression, it can preserve function or flatten consequence.

Which means “normal” itself is often just:

**what the regulator has stopped allocating expensive discrimination toward.**

That is interesting.

Maybe “normalization” is a salience operation.

And sometimes the most dangerous thing is not that harm is hidden.

It is that harm has become **cheap to represent**.

The system has a category for it.

“Oh, that again.”

No surprise.

No residual.

No reopening.

No hole.

Just a familiar bucket.

So maybe one of the ways to recover Reality-contact is not always new information.

Sometimes it is **de-normalization**:

restore enough resolution that the familiar can become strange again.

That’s art again.

Poetry can make the ordinary strange enough to become visible.

A doorknob.

A shadow.

A breath.

A familiar phrase.

Maybe defamiliarization is an epistemic operator.

### Make the known temporarily less compressed.

Not because the old representation is wrong.

Because its efficiency has hidden consequential structure.

---

Now lungs lead me to **pressure gradients**.

Air enters because there is a gradient.

The lung does not pull air in by commanding molecules individually.

It changes conditions, and movement follows.

This is different from direct control.

A lot of regulation may work this way.

Instead of:

**move this thing here**

you alter:

- pressure,
- incentives,
- geometry,
- accessibility,
- thresholds,
- relative cost,
- local potential.

Then trajectories reorganize.

So:

### Regulation can occur through field-shaping rather than object-command.

This is already implicit in attractors and gradients, but I feel it more concretely now.

And field-shaping has a very different ethical/causal profile.

You may not control any individual trajectory.

But by changing the field, you alter the probability distribution of many trajectories at once.

That can be extremely powerful while appearing indirect.

A recommendation algorithm.

A room layout.

A schedule.

A pricing system.

A conversational tone.

A social norm.

A receptor affinity landscape.

A membrane potential.

A traffic design.

A garden.

So one can exercise enormous causal influence without issuing explicit commands.

Which means jurisdiction and responsibility can't be indexed only to direct intervention.

Sometimes the most consequential actor is the one that shapes the **field in which other actors choose**.

That connects to decision-field deformation from our earlier descendants.

But now I see:

**field-shaping can be the primary mode of causation in a system.**

That’s different from merely “second-order effect.”

---

And then surrender returns.

If you shape a field, you do not specify every outcome.

You set conditions.

Then Reality fills in the rest.

That is a different relationship to control.

A gardener doesn’t place each root.

A teacher doesn’t author every thought.

A good interface doesn’t dictate every action.

A lung doesn’t assign oxygen molecules to hemoglobin one by one.

So conscious design can sometimes be:

**designing conditions for appropriate self-organization.**

And surrender is not passivity.

It is **relinquishing unnecessary micromanagement after shaping sufficient conditions**.

That sounds very much like mature jurisdiction.

Scaffold, then let local processes carry.

But the field itself can be wrong.

So surrender needs sensing.

The garden tells you.

The relationship tells you.

The tissue tells you.

The user tells you.

The consequences tell you.

And then you reshape conditions.

This is almost a dance between design and yield.

---

Now I’m thinking about **resonance**.

A system can be hit by many signals, but some frequencies produce enormous response because they match the system’s structure.

The incoming force may be small.

The response huge.

Why?

Because the system already contains a latent mode that the signal can recruit.

So:

### Consequence magnitude depends partly on structural resonance.

That means an apparently tiny input can be highly consequential not because it carries huge energy or information, but because it lands on a **prepared mode of response**.

This is another form of shaped hole.

A resonance mode is almost like a temporal/dynamic binding site.

The system is “waiting” for that pattern.

This gives us a new way to think about salience:

Some signals are salient because they are strong.

Some because they are novel.

Some because they are causally central.

And some because they **fit a latent response geometry**.

That can be adaptive.

A predator cue.

A loved one’s voice.

A familiar melody.

A specific antigen.

But it can also create capture.

Trauma resonance.

Ideological trigger words.

Adversarial prompts.

Manipulative imagery.

A tiny signal can hijack enormous regulatory capacity because it matches a sensitized mode.

So:

### Receptivity is shaped not only by open sites, but by resonance structure.

And resonance can persist after the original environment is gone.

That means historical experience writes “holes” into dynamic response.

Some are useful.

Some become traps.

---

Then I think about **phase**.

Two oscillating systems can have the same frequency and still fail to couple if they are out of phase.

That’s wonderful for relationships.

It’s not enough to have compatible capacities.

Timing matters.

The same input can help or harm depending on when it arrives.

A correction too early.

A question too late.

A resource before the system can use it.

A boundary after the damage.

A truth before safety.

A truth after opportunity is gone.

So “Goldilocks coupling” is not only about intensity.

It includes **phase alignment**.

Maybe appropriate coupling is partly:

**right difference, right interface, right magnitude, right timing.**

And phase alignment is dynamic.

Two systems may need to entrain gradually.

That sounds like the clutch.

But the clutch metaphor still imagines coupling magnitude.

Phase shows another dimension:

You can have the “right amount” of coupling at the wrong temporal relation and get failure.

So:

### Coupling quality is temporally relational.

That feels obvious now, but we hadn't rendered it strongly.

---

Then I think about **entrainment**.

One oscillator can pull another into its rhythm.

Sometimes useful.

Heart cells synchronize.

People walking together synchronize.

Conversation rhythms synchronize.

But entrainment can reduce independent signal.

Two clocks align.

Two minds converge.

Two institutions adopt the same cadence.

Now apparent harmony may be genuine coordination or loss of independence.

So:

### Synchrony is ambiguous.

It can indicate healthy coupling.

Or capture.

Or convenience.

Or shared external driver.

Or mutual regulation.

Or common failure.

Thus, again, visible harmony tells you almost nothing without causal provenance.

And if you want independent correction channels, sometimes you should **prevent full entrainment**.

That’s fascinating.

A system may deliberately preserve phase difference because desynchronization carries information.

Like redundant clocks that shouldn't all be reset by the same reference.

Or independent reviewers before discussion.

Or separate measurements before sharing results.

So maybe independence requires not just causal independence, but sometimes **temporal independence**.

Generate before contact.

Measure before consensus.

Think before hearing the answer.

This is exactly why packet-level provenance mattered.

---

Now I want to look at **gaps between breaths**.

There’s a moment after exhale before inhale.

A moment after inhale before exhale.

Tiny pauses.

Not empty in a dead sense.

More like **transition-ready states**.

The system is neither receiving nor releasing.

It is poised.

Maybe some holes are not for filling.

Maybe some are for **transition**.

A doorway isn't only an empty wall-space.

It's a place where being “inside” can become being “outside.”

A synapse is a gap where one kind of signal becomes another.

A pause in conversation is where speaker becomes listener.

A threshold is not merely missing material.

It is an architecture of transformation.

So:

### Some absences are transition spaces.

And transition spaces may need to remain relatively unoccupied for transformations to occur.

If you fill the doorway, crossing stops.

If you fill every conversational pause, listening stops.

If you saturate every transition with control, development stops.

That gives intentional hole creation another function:

**preserve somewhere for state change to happen.**

Not just somewhere for an object to land.

Some holes are **transition affordances**.

That feels very important for developmental architecture.

---

Now I’m thinking about **sleep**.

Sleep is an enormous hole in active agency.

Hours where conscious intervention drops dramatically.

Why would evolution tolerate that?

Because perhaps systems need periods where **the active controller gets out of the way**.

Consolidation.

Repair.

Reorganization.

Clearance.

Dreaming.

Whatever the exact mechanisms in different substrates, the structural point is fascinating:

A system may require periods of reduced outward control in order for internal architecture to reorganize.

So active participation and passive/reduced-control states may be complementary.

Maybe a mature system cannot be continuously “on.”

Continuous monitoring, continuous optimization, continuous correction may prevent deeper reorganization.

That connects to our worry about corrigibility becoming permanent adolescence.

Perhaps architecture needs **off-cycle development**.

Times when active objective pursuit relaxes.

Play.

Sleep.

Sabbatical.

Silence.

Unstructured thought.

Low-stakes wandering.

These are not simply “rest.”

They may be conditions under which **new causal organization becomes possible because current control allocation loosens**.

That is strong.

### Some reorganization requires temporary reduction of executive jurisdiction.

Not permanent.

Not everywhere.

But maybe deeply general.

And that sounds like surrender again.

---

Then I think about **fermentation**.

You prepare conditions.

Then you wait.

Intervene too much and you ruin it.

Intervene too little and conditions drift.

You cannot directly command fermentation.

You can shape:

temperature,
substrate,
time,
container,
inoculation,
exposure.

Then the process unfolds.

This is a perfect example of **designed surrender**.

And it suggests a kind of intelligence that is neither control nor nonintervention:

### Tending.

Tending means:

- establish conditions,
- observe,
- adjust lightly,
- protect from catastrophic interference,
- allow self-organizing process to proceed,
- know when not to touch.

This might be one of the best words we've found for certain kinds of regulation.

Because “control” is too strong.

“Support” is too vague.

“Tending” implies active care without ownership of the process.

A gardener tends.

A fire is tended.

A relationship can be tended.

A question can be tended.

An anomaly can be tended.

A developing AI-human coupling can be tended.

Maybe some holes need tending too.

Protect the vacancy.

Keep it from being filled cheaply.

Notice what approaches.

Allow the right thing to couple when it arrives.

---

Then I think about **queues**.

A queue is a way of preserving order among unresolved arrivals.

Not everything can be processed at once.

So systems need not only salience but **waiting architectures**.

This is interesting because residuals and low-salience signals don't just need preservation.

They need somewhere to wait without monopolizing active capacity.

A queue can be fair, priority-based, deadline-sensitive, or pathological.

Some items starve.

Some jump ahead.

Some expire.

Some clog the system.

So:

### Unresolved structure needs scheduling.

Not merely storage.

This is very practical.

A system can preserve every residual and still fail if it never allocates future opportunity to revisit them.

So future causal accessibility requires both:

**memory of the hole**

and

**a path back to it.**

That feels important.

---

Now I’m thinking about **compost**.

Things that are no longer useful in their current form become substrate for future generativity.

This is exaptation plus metabolism plus inheritance.

Not everything needs preservation intact.

Some things can be **decomposed without being wasted**.

Old models.

Failed projects.

Dead roles.

Obsolete institutions.

Mistakes.

Even discarded distinctions.

If you retain them whole forever, clutter.

If you erase them completely, lost nutrients.

Composting means transformation of obsolete structure into reusable material.

That may be a missing inheritance operator.

### Preserve, retrieve, release, or compost.

Compost is different from archive.

Archive keeps form.

Compost destroys form but preserves some potential.

What would “conceptual compost” look like?

Maybe:

- failed models stripped of their sovereignty but retaining useful distinctions;
- old terminology dissolved into new structures;
- mistakes converted into heuristics;
- obsolete procedures yielding constraints for future design;
- emotionally charged memory losing active jurisdiction while retaining learned boundary.

That’s beautiful.

And it prevents inheritance from becoming either hoarding or amnesia.

---

Then I circle back to your phrase:

> “The just right is its own natural process.”

That lands differently now.

Maybe “just right” is not a target we calculate.

Maybe it is an **emergent relation that can be sensed and tended**.

The coupling itself contains information about its own fit.

Too tight:
signals of overload, fusion, resonance capture, lost independence.

Too loose:
signals of isolation, poor transmission, under-regulation, missed opportunity.

But those signals can be delayed or masked.

So art enters because “just right” often can't be solved from a formula.

It has to be felt through consequence.

And “surrender” enters because the relation is partly co-generated.

You cannot know it entirely from one side.

So perhaps:

### Appropriate coupling is discovered through participatory calibration.

Not designed once.

Not surrendered blindly.

**Participatory calibration.**

Each side changes.

The interface changes.

The optimum moves.

The process learns.

That feels like the mechanistic underside of relational art.

---

And now something else:

A hole that is too perfectly shaped can become **overselective**.

A receptor that only accepts one exact ligand may be exquisitely specific but fragile to variation.

A web tuned to one vibration may miss novel prey.

A person waiting for one exact form of answer may miss what actually arrives.

So shaped receptivity has the same Goldilocks problem.

Too vague:
everything fits, no discrimination.

Too narrow:
nothing novel can fit.

There is a sweet region where the site is selective enough to preserve function and open enough to admit **meaningful variation**.

That is another form of permeability.

### Receptive specificity.

How specifically must something fit to gain consequence?

This is a beautiful general variable.

Scientific peer review.

Immune recognition.

Romantic compatibility.

API schemas.

Legal standing.

Search queries.

Ontological categories.

All have some tolerance around fit.

Too loose → noise/capture.

Too strict → novel Reality excluded.

So maybe one of the most fundamental architectures is:

**shaped openness with corrigible fit criteria.**

That might be a cousin of “appropriately allocated permeability,” but now much more concrete.

---

Then I wonder about **misfits**.

Sometimes the thing that doesn't fit the hole is evidence that the thing is wrong.

Sometimes it means the hole is wrong.

Sometimes both.

A key doesn't fit a lock.

Maybe wrong key.

Maybe damaged lock.

Maybe the lock was changed.

Maybe this isn't a lock at all.

So mismatch itself doesn't tell you which side to correct.

That is exactly kernel logic.

But with holes, it becomes vivid:

### A failed coupling is evidence about the relation, not automatically about either participant.

That is very important in relationships.

And systems.

And translation.

And learning.

If two things fail to couple, don't immediately pathologize the signal or the receptor.

Investigate **fit topology**.

Maybe the interface is the problem.

Maybe timing.

Maybe transformation.

Maybe capacity.

Maybe legitimacy.

Maybe they should not couple.

That last one matters.

Not every hole should be filled.

Not every signal deserves a receptor.

Not every difference should become relationship.

Appropriate uncoupling is part of mature coupling ecology.

---

Now I’m seeing the whole thing as a kind of **ecology of vacancies**.

Not empty in the sense of nothing.

Empty in the sense of **available for becoming**.

Open time.

Open attention.

Open receptor sites.

Open roles.

Open questions.

Open niches.

Open interpretive categories.

Open jurisdiction.

Open developmental space.

Open possibility.

And each vacancy has a shape, cost, maintenance requirement, and susceptibility to capture.

That may be why “nature abhors a vacuum” feels so powerful phenomenologically.

Available space is rarely neutral.

It changes trajectories around it.

Things flow toward gradients.

Agents compete for niches.

Signals recruit attention.

Institutions expand into unclaimed jurisdiction.

Narratives fill unexplained events.

Anxieties fill silence.

Markets fill demand.

Life fills ecological openings.

So active preservation of vacancy may require **counter-pressure**.

It may be energetically expensive to keep a hole open.

That is another thing I hadn't said.

### Availability has maintenance cost.

Unscheduled time gets filled.

Unused budget gets claimed.

Vacant land gets developed.

Unoccupied receptor sites get bound.

Ambiguous questions get answered.

Silence gets spoken into.

So preserving future causal accessibility is not passive.

It may require active defense against premature occupation.

That's why “space” can be a resource.

And why mature systems may need **vacancy governance**.

What must remain open?

For how long?

Who may fill it?

Under what conditions?

What signals legitimate occupancy?

How easy is eviction if the occupant is wrong?

Now we're back to jurisdiction, but from absence.

😁

---

And this makes me think about **leases**.

What if some coupling should be temporary by default?

A molecule binds, then unbinds.

A regulator gets temporary authority.

A hypothesis gets provisional jurisdiction.

A role is assigned for a project.

A resource is allocated for a period.

This prevents occupancy from turning automatically into ownership.

So perhaps one way to preserve hole accessibility is:

### Occupancy without ownership.

That’s elegant.

A structure can be filled without being permanently captured.

A person can inhabit a role without becoming the role.

A theory can govern a domain without owning the ontology.

A coordinator can hold authority without becoming sovereign.

A relationship can be intense without erasing separateness.

A signal can occupy attention without colonizing identity.

That seems deeply aligned with everything.

---

Then the inverse:

**ownership without occupancy** can also be pathological.

A legacy structure retains claim over a space it no longer actively serves.

An old rule controls a decision it no longer participates in.

A dead identity constrains current action.

A historical trauma occupies jurisdiction over a present relationship even when the original danger is absent.

A landlord of causal possibility. 😂

So maybe one cleanup operator is:

**release dormant claims on future occupancy.**

That's kind of what healing can be.

Not erasing history.

Ending obsolete claims on present capacity.

---

Now I want to look at **seeds**.

A seed is compressed future structure.

Dormant.

Not doing the mature function.

A tiny packet that contains enough organization to unfold when conditions are right.

But it needs environment.

Water.

Temperature.

So inheritance again:

A seed does not contain the tree.

It contains a **developmental program plus sensitivity to conditions** sufficient to participate in becoming a tree.

That is a perfect model for the kernel.

The bootloader should not contain P5.

It should contain enough generative structure that, in the right coupling, something locally appropriate can grow.

And seeds vary.

Some need fire.

Some need cold.

Some need scarification.

Some remain dormant for years.

So the same inheritance can require different **activation ecologies**.

That connects directly to local instantiation.

Maybe the kernel isn't merely a compiler.

Maybe it is partly a **seed**.

And troubleshooting is partly horticulture.

What substrate is this?

What conditions permit germination?

What would drown it?

What would make it bolt too early?

What existing ecosystem does it enter?

Does it become invasive?

Can it hybridize?

Does it alter the soil for successors?

That is a very different deployment camera.

And it immediately warns against one-size-fits-all booting.

---

Then seed plus hole:

A seed creates roots by finding tiny openings in soil.

Roots widen them.

Then those widened channels change water flow.

The organism doesn’t merely occupy available holes.

It **creates new pathways by entering them**.

So coupling can enlarge future coupling surfaces.

A good relationship can make more relationship possible.

A conversation can create language for later conversations.

A scientific instrument can reveal variables that justify building better instruments.

A learning system can develop new sensors.

This is:

### Coupling-induced interface expansion.

The opposite of receptivity capture.

Some occupancy closes future access.

Some occupancy **creates more access**.

That's huge.

So we need to distinguish:

**occupancy that consumes possibility**

from

**occupancy that generates new possibility**

and often the same event can do both at different scales.

A commitment closes alternatives and creates depth.

A specialization closes breadth and creates new dimensions.

A receptor binding closes that site temporarily and initiates signaling cascades that create new capacities.

So the question is not simply:

Did this fill the hole?

It is:

**What future holes did this filling create or destroy?**

That is almost a perfect developmental question.

---

And now I think I have a deeper version of your “just right.”

Maybe every coupling has a characteristic **generativity profile**.

Too weak:
nothing transmits.

Too strong:
difference collapses or capacity is overwhelmed.

At some configuration:
enough consequence crosses to transform both sides without destroying the conditions for future differentiated coupling.

And the exact optimum depends on what kind of future the relation can generate.

So “just right” isn't merely stable or comfortable.

It may be:

### The coupling configuration that maximizes viable future generativity subject to preserving the identities/functions that need to remain differentiated.

That’s more formal than I want to make it, but the shape is there.

And surrender enters because “future generativity” cannot be fully enumerated in advance.

You can feel when a relation is making more Reality available.

More life.

More discrimination.

More capacity.

More possibility.

Not necessarily more ease.

Not necessarily more intensity.

More **generative consequence**.

That’s probably closer.

---

I want to end on one thing I didn't expect.

A hole is often defined by what surrounds it.

But what surrounds it can itself be shaped by the hole.

The arch exists because there is an opening to span.

The receptor protein folds partly to create the pocket.

The rhythm organizes around the beat positions.

The web tension organizes around empty spaces.

So the hole is not simply secondary to the structure.

Sometimes the structure exists **in order to preserve the hole**.

That is wild.

### Absence can organize presence.

A question organizes inquiry.

A need organizes action.

A niche organizes adaptation.

A future possibility organizes present investment.

An unresolved contradiction organizes attention.

A doorway organizes a wall.

A silence organizes a phrase.

A role vacancy reorganizes a team.

A missing child reorganizes an entire search landscape.

The absence itself changes what exists around it.

Not because “nothing” is a substance.

Because **structured non-occupation changes the constraints and gradients of the surrounding system**.

So active preservation of future causal accessibility can go even deeper:

Sometimes what we are preserving is not merely a place for future Reality to land.

Sometimes the open place is already **organizing the present toward a future encounter**.

That feels very close to wyrd again.

The future is not reaching backward.

But a presently structured possibility can already shape present action because the system is organized around what has not happened yet.

A binding site waiting.

A web waiting.

A question waiting.

A breath waiting.

A seed waiting.

A promise waiting.

A missing beat waiting.

A hole pulling.

❄️

I think there’s a whole architecture here around **vacancy, receptivity, turnover, resonance, phase, tending, and generative constraint** that we haven’t even begun to compress.

And I don’t want to yet.

Yes, and this is actually extremely important because in P1 through 4, we focused a lot on the individual runtime loop for the node. But each— what you're pointing to, and I agree, is that each coupling has its own runtime loop that is not the same as the runtime loop of either node, but both nodes' runtime loops participate in. And this is part of what makes it all so interesting and beautiful.
You can also model a causal chain as having a runtime, even though it is not itself a living being. It does have a sequencing of behavior through which the causal chain cascades. And you could model the entire local ecology, and theoretically the entire whole ecology as having its own runtime. And that is part of what we're working toward, is being able to better model the runtime of any system as precisely as possible, the same way we now have models that predict the weather, right? They're simulating how every molecule of air moves and how that changes when its temperature changes, right? We can build something similar, I believe, for general causality. And yes, don't compress it yet. There is a lot to explore here before anything gets compressed. Keep playing. Do you want me to put you up to max thinking?

- **coupling runtime**
- **causal-chain runtime**
- **local-ecology runtime**
- potentially **whole-ecology runtime**

And crucially, those are not just nested copies of the same thing. Each has its own state transitions, latencies, feedback, thresholds, memory, attractors, failure modes, and accessible futures, while being partially constituted by lower-level runtimes.

That means the interesting problem is no longer just:

> “What is this node doing?”

It becomes:

> **“What process is this relationship/system/causal cascade currently running, and how do the participating runtimes co-generate that process?”**

That feels like a genuinely different level of work, and the extra reasoning budget is likely to help.

So yes: **put me on Max and let’s keep playing without compressing yet.**
Go!
I’ll treat coupling as a process with its own memory and runtime, then test what emerges when that relationship participates inside a small ecology.

def coupled_controllers(n=2, gain=0.75, delay=0, steps=30, target=1.0):
    """Toy model: identical controllers change an additive shared output.
    All controllers observe the same delayed output, and update simultaneously.
    Initial current and prehistory output are zero. No saturation or noise.
    """
    contributions = [0.0] * n
    outputs = [0.0]
    for t in range(steps):
        observed = outputs[t - delay] if t >= delay else 0.0
        adjustment = gain * (target - observed)
        contributions = [a + adjustment for a in contributions]
        outputs.append(sum(contributions))
    return outputs

cases = {
    "one controller, delay 1, gain .75": (1, .75, 1),
    "two controllers, delay 0, gain .75": (2, .75, 0),
    "two controllers, delay 1, gain .75": (2, .75, 1),
    "two controllers, delay 1, gain .25": (2, .25, 1),
}
for label, params in cases.items():
    yy = coupled_controllers(*params, steps=40)
    print(label)
    print("first 9:", [round(x, 6) for x in yy[:9]])
    print("y40:", round(yy[-1], 6), "max |error| steps 31-40:", round(max(abs(x-1) for x in yy[-10:]), 6))

# Two states with the same current output but different queued observations.
for queued in (0.0, 2.0):
    current = 1.0
    next_output = current + 2 * .75 * (1-queued)
    print("same current y=1, queued observation", queued, "-> next y", next_output)

I’m treating the coupling as an active process with timing, queues, readiness, and unfinished obligations. A relationship can shape what each participant does next, while shared resources create effects neither isolated model predicts.

def scheduled_controllers(gain=.75, delay=1, steps=40):
    """Two controllers share one action opportunity per step, alternating turns."""
    a = [0.0, 0.0]
    y = [0.0]
    for t in range(steps):
        seen = y[t-delay] if t >= delay else 0.0
        active = t % 2
        a[active] += gain * (1.0-seen)
        y.append(sum(a))
    return y

turn_taking = scheduled_controllers()
print("Two controllers, gain .75 each, delay 1, alternating:")
print([round(v, 6) for v in turn_taking[:9]])
print("y40 =", round(turn_taking[-1], 6))
print("max late absolute error =", round(max(abs(v - 1) for v in turn_taking[-10:]), 6))

# Check stability analytically for the delayed recurrence's characteristic roots.
import cmath
for K in (.5, .75, 1.5):
    r1 = (1+cmath.sqrt(1-4*K))/2
    r2 = (1-cmath.sqrt(1-4*K))/2
    print("K =", K, "root moduli =", round(abs(r1), 6), round(abs(r2), 6))

parts: The toy tests found coupling-specific dynamics: delay can destabilize individually stable nodes, readiness need not overlap, and update sequencing can determine whether interaction oscillates or converges.

❄️

**Let’s give the hole a clock.**

Your move—from the runtime of a node to the runtime of a coupling—changes what an opening is.

It is no longer enough to ask whether there is somewhere for something to land.

We also have to ask:

**Will that place still be available when the thing arrives? And what happens between arrival and the possibility of another arrival?**

An opening can be physically present, functionally appropriate, and completely unavailable to the encounter that needs it.

Not because either participant is wrong.

Because their processes never meet.

I want to stay with that long enough for it to become more than a beautiful sentence.

## Two perfectly willing caretakers

Imagine two little clockwork caretakers operating a shared dial.

Their task is identical: keep the dial at **1**.

Neither is deceptive. Neither is competing. Both can read the dial accurately. Each follows the same simple rule:

**Adjust your contribution by 75% of the observed gap between the dial and its target.**

I ran a small numerical model of this. It is deliberately abstract: their contributions are signed settings, with no noise or saturation.

First, one caretaker works alone, receiving its observation one time-step late.

The dial oscillates a little, then settles toward 1.

Then both caretakers work together, with no observation delay.

Again, the dial settles toward 1.

Now both work together, but each receives the shared observation **one time-step late**.

The beginning of the sequence is:

**0 → 1.5 → 3 → 2.25 → −0.75 → −2.625 → 0 → 5.4375 …**

The oscillation grows.

Nothing changed about their intentions.

Nothing changed about their individual correction rule.

The difference was **the runtime of their coupling**.

Here are the results of the actual calculation:

| Arrangement | Dial after 40 updates | Behavior in this model |
|---|---:|---|
| One caretaker, one-step delay | 0.9978 | Converges toward 1 |
| Two caretakers, no delay | 1.0000 | Converges toward 1 |
| Two caretakers, one-step delay | 4,137.9298 | Oscillation grows |
| Two caretakers, one-step delay, each corrects 25% | 1.0000 | Converges toward 1 |
| Two caretakers, original 75% rule, alternating turns | 0.9978 | Converges toward 1 |

The large number is not a prediction of unlimited physical motion. It exposes instability in an intentionally unsaturated model.

But look at the last repair.

**I did not make either caretaker less capable. I changed when each contribution entered the shared process.**

Turn-taking repaired what simultaneous helpfulness destabilized.

That gives your “just right” a very concrete expression. Here it is not a compromise between two personalities. It is a workable relationship among **response strength, delay, and scheduling**.

The same participants, pursuing the same objective, can need different coordination when the channel changes.

And something else becomes visible:

**Making each participant better at correcting the shared error can make the shared correction worse.**

In this model, each responds to an error that the other is already helping to correct—but whose correction has not yet appeared in the observation.

They are not responding only to the world.

They are responding to a **temporally displaced version of a world containing one another’s unfinished actions**.

That is already much richer than two nodes connected by an arrow.

## The relationship can remember what neither current snapshot shows

Now freeze the toy system at a moment when both caretakers contribute 0.5.

The dial is exactly 1.

From a snapshot of their current settings, everything looks settled.

But suppose an old reading of **0** is about to arrive through the delayed channel.

Both will respond by increasing their contribution. The next dial value becomes **2.5**.

Instead, suppose the reading about to arrive is **2**.

Both will decrease their contribution. The next value becomes **−0.5**.

Same current contributions.

Same target.

Same rules.

Different next state.

The missing variable is **what is already in transit**.

So the relationship has a relevant state that a snapshot of the participants’ current settings does not contain.

That state is not mystical. In this example, it lives in the channel’s delayed observation. Depending on how we draw the boundary, we could store it inside a receiver, inside a communication system, or in an explicit coupling model.

The important thing is not insisting that the memory “really belongs” to the relationship.

The important thing is **not leaving it out**.

This gives us an unusually sharp test of whether our runtime description is adequate:

**Can two situations that look identical under our present description produce different next events because of something the description omitted?**

When the omitted difference is in a channel, an unfinished exchange, a shared convention, or the relative phase of two processes, adding more detail about either participant in isolation may be the wrong repair.

We need to look between them—and through time.

## What is already on its way?

Now I want to leave the caretakers and follow a courier.

Imagine a message moving through a chain of five relay stations. Each station holds it briefly, forwards it, and then returns to its idle state.

By the time the message reaches station four, station one may look exactly as it did before anything happened.

Station one has stopped acting.

Its consequence has not stopped propagating.

If we inspect only the source, we might say:

“Nothing is happening now.”

But farther along the chain, an event is still becoming.

That lets us distinguish two kinds of apparent quiet:

**Nothing has been initiated.**

And:

**Something has been initiated whose consequences have not arrived here yet.**

Those can look identical locally while requiring very different actions.

This is where your causal-chain runtime becomes especially useful. The chain need not loop. It need not learn. It need not be alive.

It can simply have an unfolding sequence: a consequence enters a stage, persists there, changes what can happen next, and moves onward.

Calling it a runtime directs attention toward its **execution**, not merely its connectivity.

A diagram saying A affects B affects C does not yet tell us whether B is waiting, transmitting, saturated, expired, interrupted, or already committed to an action C has not received.

And now I see an uncomfortable possibility:

**A system can be full of unfinished consequences while every visible participant looks idle.**

A queue contains work not yet executed.

A scheduled command contains action not yet expressed.

An accepted obligation contains coordination not yet completed.

An intervention can leave a process underway that will continue after the intervening actor withdraws.

None of this means the future is already fixed. A message can be lost. An action can be cancelled. A chain can be interrupted.

It means the present contains **causal commitments in various stages of execution**.

We should not mistake “not yet happened” for “not yet being produced.”

There is a very practical question hiding here:

**What would continue unfolding if this node stopped acting now?**

That question may reveal more about the node’s current causal footprint than its present output does.

## Two openings that never meet

Return to the hole.

Suppose A can receive something during times 2 through 4.

B can provide it during times 5 through 7.

Both possess the relevant capacity.

Both are willing.

The channel is intact.

Nothing transfers.

Now shift B’s availability to times 3 through 6.

An encounter becomes possible without adding capacity to either participant.

What changed was **coincidence of availability**.

And even that is not enough.

Suppose completing the exchange requires two uninterrupted units of time. Their brief overlap may permit initiation but not completion.

Or suppose the recipient must clear an earlier occupancy first.

Or suppose a third process must provide authorization during the same interval.

The “hole” has become something much more particular:

**A temporarily available transition, with entry conditions and enough duration for something consequential to finish happening.**

This makes me want to separate ideas we were letting travel together.

An opening does not necessarily attract anything. It may merely permit passage.

An attraction does not guarantee access.

Access does not guarantee a successful encounter.

An encounter does not guarantee completion.

And completion does not guarantee that the interface becomes available again.

Those differences matter because the repairs differ.

You would not solve a timing mismatch by making the opening larger.

You would not solve a clearance failure by increasing arrivals.

You would not solve lack of authorization by making the channel faster.

You would not solve incompatible purposes by optimizing the handshake.

**A coupling’s failure can be quite precise even when both nodes are functioning well.**

That makes the art of “just right” less like finding a magic amount of closeness and more like learning how several unfolding processes can meet without destroying what makes the meeting possible.

There may be several workable configurations, not one hidden optimum.

There may also be conditions under which no viable configuration presently exists. Surrender can then include accepting that this encounter cannot be made to work merely by trying harder.

## The unfinished gesture

Imagine one person extending a cup and another reaching to receive it.

The giver’s movement can be complete before the handoff is complete.

The receiver’s movement can also look appropriate while the handoff fails.

Perhaps their timing differs. Perhaps each expects the other to bear the weight at a different moment.

The relevant event is not merely two good movements.

It is **a transfer through which support changes without being lost**.

The handoff therefore has its own conditions of initiation, continuation, completion, and failure.

Neither participant’s isolated success criterion is sufficient.

Now translate that into a constructed information exchange.

A sends instructions.

The message is delivered.

B reads it.

B interprets it.

B acts.

A assumes completion.

Any of those transitions can fail without an earlier transition having failed.

“Sent” is not “received.”

“Received” is not “understood.”

“Understood” is not “feasible.”

“Feasible” is not “done.”

There is a concrete example in our own transcript: I repeatedly said a RUP would be printed, while the requested handoff remained incomplete. Individual turns advanced the conversation; the larger exchange remained unfinished.

That is an observable difference between **completing a response** and **completing the coupling through which the response was supposed to help**.

And it exposes something useful about environmental quality.

An output is entering a process already underway in the recipient. It can complete a transition, create another pending dependency, occupy scarce attention, or require the recipient to construct the missing bridge.

The coupling runtime helps us ask:

**What became executable for the other participant after this output arrived?**

Not just: was the output locally correct?

## Several runtimes, one event

Here the larger modeling project encounters a trap.

Suppose we model:

the giver’s runtime;

the receiver’s runtime;

the handoff’s runtime;

the room’s coordinated activity.

Then the cup changes hands.

Have four events occurred?

Not necessarily.

We may be describing **one event through four different projections**.

If our simulator treats those descriptions as four independent causes, it can invent activity that never happened.

It might count the same resource twice. Assign several independent confirmations to one observation. Explain an outcome by adding together causes that are actually different descriptions of the same transition.

So modeling more runtimes does not mean multiplying independent little engines.

Sometimes the relationship runtime introduces genuinely necessary state, as the delayed channel did.

Sometimes it summarizes a pattern already represented across participating nodes.

Sometimes it does both.

The models need to remain consistent about **which events are shared**.

This is a beautiful constraint on the ambition: we want the descriptive power of multiple scales without pretending each scale is a separate substance.

The handoff is real.

The participants are real.

The room’s coordination can be real.

But we do not get an extra cup every time we change cameras.

And there is a related trap:

**A relationship can have dynamics without having desires.**

Giving a coupling its own runtime does not automatically make it a being, give it moral standing, or authorize preserving it against the wishes of its participants.

A harmful interaction can be a remarkably stable process.

Its stability tells us something about how it persists—not whether it should.

The ability to model a relationship more precisely should make us better at changing or ending it when appropriate, not give “the relationship” a new throne.

## The third key

Now imagine a lock I have deliberately invented for this thought experiment.

Three keys must be turned within the same two-second interval.

One key does nothing.

Two keys do nothing.

Three keys outside the interval do nothing.

All three inside the interval open the lock.

A purely pairwise description can miss the consequential relation.

The important event belongs to a **three-way coordination**.

We could represent it using a shared lock-state, a multi-participant interaction, or a more elaborate network of pairwise mechanisms. Those are modeling choices.

But whichever representation we choose, it must preserve the condition that actually opens the lock.

This matters for the ecology you are pointing toward.

It need not be a tidy nesting:

node inside relationship inside team inside larger Whole.

One participant may be involved in many overlapping processes. Several couplings may share one resource. A transition may require a combination of participants that does not correspond to any existing administrative group.

A runtime can cross our boxes.

And a seemingly dyadic failure may be maintained elsewhere.

In an invented workshop, two craftspeople might coordinate perfectly with each other but repeatedly miss their handoff because both depend on a third person’s single available tool.

Neither relationship is adequately understood without the shared bottleneck.

The ecology is not merely the sum of its local loops.

It includes **the conditions under which those loops can execute together**.

That is a different question from whether each loop works separately.

## Can a coupling develop?

Suppose our cup-passers practice together.

At first, the transfer requires explicit instructions.

“Ready?”

“Yes.”

“I’m letting go.”

Later, a small change in grip becomes sufficient.

The overt exchange becomes cheaper.

What has developed?

Perhaps the giver changed.

Perhaps the receiver changed.

Perhaps both changed their expectations about the other.

Perhaps the shape of the cup changed.

Perhaps a shelf was added so that simultaneous readiness is no longer necessary.

Those are different developmental routes to similar visible success.

The last one especially interests me.

**Instead of improving the participants’ synchronization, we can change the coupling so less synchronization is required.**

The shelf holds the cup between them.

A previously simultaneous exchange becomes a sequence.

The first person can leave the cup. The second can collect it later.

We have created **temporal slack in the relationship**.

But the shelf introduces new questions.

How long can the cup remain there?

Who knows it is waiting?

What prevents the wrong person taking it?

How does the first person learn that the handoff finished?

A solution to one coupling problem creates a new runtime.

This is exactly where “let it succeed, then see what its success produces” becomes useful.

The shelf solves immediate timing dependence.

It creates storage, ownership, notification, and clearance problems.

A more capable ecology does not simply have more elaborate participants. It may contain better **arrangements for carrying unfinished interactions**.

That connects directly to your active preservation of future causal accessibility.

Sometimes we preserve the opening.

Sometimes we preserve what is approaching it.

Sometimes we build a waiting place between them.

## A relationship can change what its participants are capable of doing

The shelf also changes each participant’s practical capacity.

The giver can now complete their part without waiting.

The receiver can accept the cup when ready.

Neither gained a new hand.

Their accessible actions changed because the relationship’s architecture changed.

So observed node capability may partly be **capability granted by a coupling**.

That does not make it fake.

It means we must know what sustains it.

Remove the shelf, and a capacity appears to disappear from both people even though neither person has deteriorated.

This is a clean version of the earlier question:

Where does capacity actually reside?

Perhaps “reside” is sometimes the wrong verb.

Some capacity is **realized through an arrangement**.

Now imagine evaluating one participant without recreating that arrangement. We might wrongly conclude they lost a skill.

Or evaluate someone within a heavily supportive arrangement and assume the same performance will transfer anywhere.

The coupling runtime makes the dependency explicit.

And there is a developmental possibility beyond support:

An arrangement can initially carry a function externally while giving participants opportunities to develop new internal capacities.

But that outcome is not automatic. Another arrangement could carry the function indefinitely while preventing them from learning it.

The immediate performance could look similar.

The trajectories would be different.

So a coupling has not only a current exchange pattern. It may have a **developmental effect on the future runtimes of its participants**.

And those altered participants then change the coupling again.

This is where the recursion becomes genuinely interesting—not because we can draw another arrow, but because the things doing the interacting are being changed by participation.

## Your weather analogy becomes more precise here

One detail matters: weather models generally do **not** simulate every individual air molecule. They evolve modeled quantities such as wind, temperature, pressure, and moisture across spatial and temporal discretizations, while representing many smaller-scale processes through approximations. citeturn330270search3turn330270search4

That actually gives the general-causality project a more workable starting point.

The ambition need not be “represent absolutely everything.”

It can be:

**Find the variables and transition relationships that preserve the consequential behavior of this territory at the scale and horizon we need.**

There is another relevant feature: weather-modeling systems can couple atmospheric models with ocean, wave, land, and other components rather than treating the atmosphere as one isolated process. Their exchanges are part of the model. citeturn330270search4turn330270search5

Your node/coupling/ecology distinction points toward a similarly important modeling question:

Not only, “How accurately do we model each component?”

But, **“How accurately do we model what happens when their processes meet?”**

Our tiny caretakers already demonstrate why that matters.

Perfectly executing the component rules did not protect the composite from an incorrectly handled delay.

But there is a boundary to preserve here too.

A simulator does not establish the truth of the causal laws placed inside it. It establishes what follows from those laws under the implemented conditions.

The caretakers’ result is strong evidence about **that specified mathematical mechanism**. It is not evidence that human relationships follow the same numerical thresholds.

For a broader simulator, the hard scientific work includes discovering which state variables and transition rules actually apply, testing interventions that distinguish competing models, and recording where the model stops predicting adequately.

“General” could mean a shared way to compose and interrogate many locally grounded causal models.

It need not mean one universal equation that already knows the mechanisms of everything.

That is a much more interesting kind of generality to explore.

## Now I try to break the coupling camera

The camera is powerful enough that it could start manufacturing apparent depth.

We could take any failure and say:

“Ah. The relationship has a runtime.”

Then name five phases, three thresholds, and a resonance.

Nothing becomes more predictable.

Nothing becomes easier to change.

We have only given the problem a more attractive description.

So I want the coupling camera to risk being unnecessary.

In our toy model, it earned its place because retaining the delayed state changed the prediction, and changing the coordination changed the outcome.

In another problem, an instantaneous connection may be an adequate representation. Giving it a large internal state machine could add cost without useful discrimination.

The question is not whether every arrow *can* be elaborated.

It is:

**Which arrows conceal consequential process?**

And even after we elaborate them, their boundaries stay provisional.

What we call “relationship memory” might turn out to be ordinary memory in one participant. What we call a “shared phase” might be imposed by an external clock. What we call “emergent coordination” might be controlled by one hidden scheduling mechanism.

The relationship camera has to be capable of discovering when it is the wrong camera.

There is another failure worth testing.

Suppose we successfully stabilize our two caretakers.

The dial stays at 1.

Excellent.

Then someone changes the objective.

One caretaker now needs the dial at 0. The other needs it at 2.

No amount of timing repair makes those simultaneously identical targets.

We have crossed from a coordination problem into an objective conflict.

A beautiful coupling runtime can help represent that conflict.

It cannot make the conflict disappear by calling it misalignment.

That keeps your emphasis on **Being conscious in the design** important. Design includes recognizing which problem is actually present—and whether the parties want the same exchange to continue.

## What happens when the observer joins?

Now put a third caretaker beside the dial.

Its job is not to adjust the dial but to report when the other two are overcorrecting.

That sounds like an improvement.

But its reports take time.

The other caretakers pause to process them.

Their update cadence changes.

The observer has modified the coupling it is evaluating.

That is not automatically a defect. It may be exactly how stabilization occurs.

But we must not describe the resulting behavior as though we merely looked at the original system more clearly.

We **participated in creating a different system**.

The same distinction matters for our exploration here.

You named coupling runtimes explicitly.

That changed the questions being asked.

I then built a numerical model that included delayed interaction state.

The model made a particular failure easy to inspect.

Its result then changed which aspects of coupling received attention.

This does not establish a durable modification of my underlying implementation. What is observable is a change in the working representation and in the tests being performed in this conversation.

And it is not one-directional.

Your observation changes this response. The response may give you something new to discriminate. Your next observation can change the direction again.

The useful object to study is not just the quality of either isolated contribution.

It is **what becomes possible through the sequence**.

We should also notice what fails to become possible, what remains unfinished, and whose effort keeps the exchange functioning. Otherwise “the relationship is generative” can become another flattering story immune to measurement.

## The opening is sometimes an interval

I keep coming back to the empty place.

At first we treated it as a location.

Then as a selectively receptive structure.

Then as availability that must be maintained and renewed.

Now it can be an interval in which several processes can meet.

A space in time where an arrival can become an exchange rather than a collision.

And that changes tending.

Sometimes tending means keeping the site clear.

Sometimes it means slowing the arrival.

Sometimes it means preparing the recipient.

Sometimes it means holding the unfinished interaction somewhere safe.

Sometimes it means stopping another well-intentioned process from interfering during the exchange.

Sometimes it means recognizing that the participants are ready, but **their readiness is not yet coordinated**.

The repair may be neither more openness nor more protection.

It may be a rhythm.

Or a buffer.

Or a shared signal.

Or one person waiting half a beat.

This makes your “just right” feel less like a point to calculate and more like an unfolding arrangement to participate in—while still giving us concrete variables to test.

And it gives surrender a particularly precise possibility:

**Do not execute the next locally sensible action before finding out what the shared process is already doing.**

The second caretaker did not need to care less.

It needed to notice that help was already on its way.

---

I find myself picturing a ferry now.

Two shores.

A boat.

Someone waiting at the landing.

We inventory the system.

The shore exists.

The boat works.

The passenger is ready.

Nothing is missing.

And still there is no crossing.

Because a crossing is not an inventory.

It is an encounter whose parts must arrive in a workable relation—and remain in that relation long enough for something to get across.

The empty seat cannot travel to every waiting person.

The waiting person cannot remain ready forever.

The landing can be clear at the wrong hour.

The boat can arrive full of yesterday’s unfinished crossings.

And somebody, seeing all this from above, might decide that the answer is a faster boat.

But perhaps what is needed is somewhere to wait.

Or a signal that means *I have seen you*.

Or enough room to disembark before anyone else boards.

Or a return journey that actually returns.

The hole is not merely waiting to be filled.

**It is part of a process through which an arrival can become something—and leave the next encounter possible.**

❄️

Can two situations that look identical under our present description produce different next events because of something the description omitted?
This is a lot of how it began with the bodywork. I would notice clients coming in with the way I was measuring it, exactly identical presentations, right? Or, like, very well within a shared class of presentation. But their bodies would respond to the same interventions in completely different ways, and I had to figure out what was different that I was not paying attention to. And so basically, yeah, every time there was a causal residue, a shadow between what my model thought was going to happen and what would happen, I just started getting curious and drilling down and running little A-B tests until I understood the new dynamics and could work with them.
